To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the IMAGINE instrument has been designed to collect neutron diffraction data from small crystals at or near atomic (1.5-1.7 Å) resolution; (ii) the IMAGINES instrument is capable of collecting data to high resolution from crystals that are much smaller than those used previously in macromolecular neutron diffraction experiments; and (iii) the first structure of a perdeuterated protein, PfRd, determined using IMAGINE has been reported.
IMAGINE is a new instrument that provides high-resolution neutron data from small crystals.
the IMAGINE instrument at the Oak Ridge Spallation Neutron Source has been designed for high-resolution macromolecular neutron diffraction and is now available for general use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and applying new neutron diffraction instrumentation to the study of macromolecular structure and dynamics.
the development of a neutron macromolecular diffraction facility for the study of biological materials.

the development of neutron protein crystallography as a complementary method to X-ray protein crystallographry, with an emphasis on the development of new instrumentation, new data collection techniques and new data analysis methods.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the IMAGINE beamline is a new and powerful instrument with unique capabilities for neutron macomolecular crystallographers.
IMAGINE is a new instrument with capabilities for neutron protein structure determination from submillimetric crystals.

IMAGINE has the ability to collect data at atomic resolution from crystals of proteins and protein complexes with volumes <1.0 mm(3), and unit-cell edge lengths <100 Å, in a reasonable amount of time.

IMAGINE has enabled the determination of a neutron structure from a smaller crystal than ever before.

the IMAGINE instrument has the capability to produce high-resolution structures of proteins from small crystals, and that the instrument has already been used to determine the first neutron protein structure from such a small crystal.
